text: We don't know their kings, their gods, or what they called themselves.
Oddly, nobody has found grand palaces or giant royal tombs either.
Just well-planned cities built for ordinary people.
Then around 1900 BCE, the great cities slowly emptied.
Rivers shifted course, one may have dried up, the monsoon grew weaker,
However, people drifted into villages, and the drains filled with mud.
So here's the first answer to our question.
This land's first great treasure wasn't stolen at all.
Nature took it back.
But over the mountains in the northwest, new people were coming, and they carried something
they would guard more carefully than gold, hymns so sacred that for more than three
years, nobody was allowed to write them down.
The culture that grew up in North India is known by its sacred hymns, the Vedas.
The oldest, the Rig Veda, is more than 3,000 years old.
Where its composers came from is one of the most argued-about questions in Indian history.
Many historians, using clues from languages and ancient DNA, think speakers of an Indo
Aryan language arrived gradually from Central Asia and mixed with people already here. Others
argue the culture grew mostly from within India. The debate is very much alive.
What nobody argues about is this. The Vedas were memorized, sound for sound. Priests trained
from childhood to chant them forwards, backwards, in pairs, and in triplets, so not a single
syllable would change. UNESCO now lists that chanting as part of humanity's
heritage. Again, from the beginning, backwards this time. Guruji, we've done
this hymn 40 times. And tomorrow, we do it 40 more. Can't we just write it down?
Write it down and trust a leaf?
